design_detail: Short review (5 pages, 13 references, 7 of them the author's) in Current Directions in Psychological Science, by the main proponent of the Pavlovian conditioning account of drug tolerance and withdrawal. It argues that cues paired with a drug come to elicit compensatory responses that oppose the drug's effect, so that tolerance depends on the setting (situational specificity) and withdrawal symptoms and craving appear when the cues occur without the drug; it extends the account to internal cues (the act of self-administration; the first effects of a dose) and to treatment (cue exposure). The evidence is mainly rat experiments from the author's laboratory, with a few human laboratory examples and clinical observations, all described without numbers. No search or appraisal. Overdose in people is not discussed.
can_establish: What the conditioning account of tolerance and withdrawal proposes and predicts, and which experiments, mostly in rats, its author offered in support as of 2005.
cannot_establish: Whether unfamiliar settings or cues change overdose risk in people (the review presents no human overdose data), how large situation-specific effects are in people (no effect sizes are given), or whether the proposed form of cue-exposure treatment works (no trial is cited).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). The cited studies are mostly rat experiments with alcohol and morphine from the author's laboratory; the human examples are college students drinking alcohol in a familiar or an unfamiliar drink, caffeine taken as coffee or intravenously, alcohol-experienced people denied alcohol after self-administering or receiving it passively (Mello & Mendelson, 1970), and clinical observations of craving and withdrawal on meeting drug cues (Kolb, 1927).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria; the studies were chosen by the author.
sample.selection_effects: The evidence is selected by the originator of the model; the human studies are few and each is described in one sentence, without sample sizes or effect sizes.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable. The cited experiments manipulate where or how a drug is given (the usual environment versus a different one; self-administered versus given by the experimenter; a small dose before a large one); details are not given in the review.

comparison.controls: In the cited experiments: animals tested in a different environment, yoked animals receiving the same doses passively, and unpaired controls; in the human examples, an unfamiliar drink, or the intravenous route, compared with the usual drink.

outcomes.instruments: As cited, without detail: body temperature (alcohol and morphine in rats), analgesia, behavioural and thermic signs of morphine withdrawal in rats, the cardiac effect of caffeine, alcohol intoxication, and reports of withdrawal distress and craving.
outcomes.operationalization: Tolerance: a smaller drug effect after repeated administration. Situational specificity: more tolerance when the drug is given where it was given before than in a different environment, where the effect is partly or fully restored (Fig. 1, p. 297). Withdrawal symptoms: the same conditional compensatory responses, expressed when the usual cues occur without the drug.

analysis.effect_sizes: None. The review gives directions of effect only, with no sample size, effect size or test for any cited study.
analysis.selective_reporting: No study that failed to find situational specificity is cited, and other contributions to tolerance are not discussed, although the review says only that conditioning contributes to tolerance (p. 297). The statement that relapse and withdrawal are frequently precipitated by small doses is called well established with one citation of the author's own work (p. 299).

interpretation_gap.results_show: A coherent model supported in the review mainly by rat experiments from the author's laboratory, a few human laboratory demonstrations (alcohol in a familiar versus an unfamiliar drink; caffeine by mouth versus intravenously) and clinical observations, all reported without numbers.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that conditional responses mediate the expression of tolerance and withdrawal symptoms and that treatment should incorporate learning principles to extinguish cue–drug associations (p. 296). The treatment section predicts that cue-exposure therapy would be more effective if it also included drug-onset and self-administration cues, citing no trial (p. 299). For overdose, the review supplies the mechanism (tolerance that depends on drug-paired cues, including tolerance to lethal effects in many species, citing Siegel et al., 2000; p. 297) but no evidence from people.

timeline.event: Kolb, first superintendent of the narcotics treatment farm in Lexington, Kentucky, described craving, withdrawal symptoms and relapse when treated patients met situations paired with their drug use (as cited, p. 296).
Mello & Mendelson: alcohol-experienced people denied alcohol showed more severe withdrawal after self-administering than after programmed drinking (as cited, p. 298).
The author's interviews with 10 overdose survivors in methadone maintenance (not cited in this review)

Siegel, Baptista, Kim, McDonald & Weise-Kelly: review of the associative basis of tolerance, the source cited for situational specificity across effects, including lethal effects, drugs and species (as cited, p. 297).
McDonald & Siegel: rats with a history of large morphine doses showed behavioural and thermic withdrawal signs when given a small dose (as described, pp. 298–299).

replication.where_it_stands: A concise statement of the conditioning account by its main proponent. Its support is largely experimental work in rats; it presents no human data on overdose and no trial of the treatment it proposes. Cite it for the model and its predictions, including that cue-elicited responses are compensatory (opposite to the drug's effect), with primary studies for any figures.

funding.funder: Acknowledgments: some research summarized in the article was supported by grants from the National Institute on Drug Abuse and the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (p. 299).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Single author (McMaster University) reviewing his own research programme: 7 of the 13 references and all four recommended readings are his. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: For overdose: case-crossover studies comparing the circumstances of fatal and non-fatal overdoses with the same people's ordinary occasions of use. For the mechanism in people: laboratory studies in people with opioid tolerance that measure an opioid response (for example pupil size or pain sensitivity) with familiar versus unfamiliar drug cues. For treatment: randomized trials of cue exposure that includes internal cues against standard care.

domains.note: No search, dates or criteria; a short-format review of the author's own research programme.
No study is appraised; sample sizes, effect sizes and replications are not given.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: 7 of 13 references and all four recommended readings are the author's; the central demonstrations (self-administration cues, drug-onset cues, small-dose-elicited withdrawal) come from his laboratory.
Experiments are described as experiments, but the treatment proposal is presented as following from the model without trial evidence, and one consensus claim rests on a single self-citation.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against a conditioning account of tolerance and withdrawal
domains.note: No negative findings and no competing or complementary (non-associative) mechanisms of tolerance are discussed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). This is a clear statement of the model by its originator, unsystematic and one-sided by design. Cite it for what the model proposes and predicts and as a pointer to the experiments; any claim about the size of the effect, or about overdose in people, needs primary human evidence, which this review does not provide.

key_findings.finding: The model: cues that accompany taking a drug act as conditional stimuli and the drug's effect as the unconditional stimulus; after repeated pairings the cues come to elicit compensatory responses that counteract the drug's effect, and these conditional compensatory responses produce tolerance, which grows as the drug is taken more often.
key_findings.locator: Pavlovian Conditioning and Drug Effects, 1st paragraph (p. 296, right column); Pavlovian Conditioning and Drug Tolerance, 1st paragraph (begins p. 296, continues on p. 297 at 'Tolerance is said to occur')

key_findings.finding: Example given for a conditional compensatory response: rats tolerant to alcohol's temperature-lowering effect developed a rise in body temperature when given an inert substance with alcohol-associated cues (Siegel et al., 2000).
key_findings.locator: Pavlovian Conditioning and Drug Effects, 1st paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Situational specificity of tolerance: after repeated doses in one environment, tolerance is apparent when the drug is given in that environment, but is attenuated (the drug effect partly or completely reinstated) when it is given in a different environment. The review states this has been seen for tolerance to a variety of effects, including lethal effects, of various drugs in many species (citing Siegel et al., 2000).
key_findings.locator: Fig. 1 and its legend; Pavlovian Conditioning and Drug Tolerance, 2nd paragraph ('A phenomenon that highlights…', left column, continuing at the top of the right column)
key_findings.note: The lethal-effects statement is a one-sentence summary citing the author's group's review; no study, species or figure is given here.

key_findings.finding: Human examples, given without numbers: college students showed more tolerance to the intoxicating effect of alcohol drunk in a familiar beer-flavoured drink than to the same amount in an unfamiliar blue, peppermint-flavoured drink; tolerance to the cardiac effect of caffeine was greater when it was taken in coffee than when the same blood level was reached intravenously.
key_findings.locator: Pavlovian Conditioning and Drug Tolerance, 3rd paragraph ('Situational specificity of tolerance has been demonstrated…', right column)
key_findings.note: Cited to Siegel et al. (2000) and Siegel, Kim & Sokolowska (2003, Circulation, 108, e38); no sample sizes or effect sizes are given.

key_findings.finding: Withdrawal symptoms are interpreted as the same conditional compensatory responses, expressed in full when the usual cues occur but the drug does not come; the review calls some withdrawal symptoms, more accurately, drug preparation symptoms, and counts craving among the less observable responses so elicited.
key_findings.locator: Pavlovian Conditioning and Drug-Withdrawal Symptoms (one paragraph, right column)
key_findings.note: The review describes cue-elicited responses only as compensatory, that is opposite to the drug's effect; it does not discuss drug-like conditioned responses, such as feeling the drug's effect before taking it.

key_findings.finding: Self-administration cues: the review states that people show more tolerance to alcohol and opiates when they self-administer than when given the same doses on a schedule set by the experimenter, and that animals that self-administer a drug by making a designated response are more tolerant than yoked animals given the same doses at the same times passively; alcohol-experienced people (Mello & Mendelson, 1970) and morphine-experienced rats (MacRae & Siegel, 1997) denied the drug showed more severe withdrawal if they had self-administered it than if they had received it passively.
key_findings.locator: Self-Administration and Tolerance (left column); Self-Administration and Withdrawal Symptoms (left column, continuing at the top of the right column)
key_findings.note: The tolerance statements are cited together to one paper from the author's group (Weise-Kelly & Siegel, 2001); no human study of opiate self-administration is named.

key_findings.finding: Drug-onset cues: in rats, a small dose of alcohol given 60 minutes before a large dose came to act as a cue, and paired rats, but not unpaired rats, were tolerant to the large dose's temperature-lowering effect (Greeley et al., 1984); rats with a history of large morphine doses showed behavioural and thermic signs of withdrawal when given a small dose (McDonald & Siegel, 2004).
key_findings.locator: Drug-Onset Cues (p. 298, right column); Drug-Onset Cues and Withdrawal Symptoms (p. 298, right column, continuing on p. 299, left column)

key_findings.finding: Cues named as able to elicit the conditional responses after treatment include the time the drug was usually taken, the people usually present, the places where it was used, tastes and odours present at the time, and, more importantly in the author's view, internal cues; merely thinking about the preferred drug is described as eliciting withdrawal distress and craving (Greeley & Ryan, 1995; Siegel & Ramos, 2002).
key_findings.locator: Implications for Treatment, 2nd paragraph ('Research concerning two types of interoceptive cues…') and 3rd paragraph ('The purpose of cue-exposure treatments…', right column)

key_findings.finding: Treatment proposal: cue-exposure therapy presents drug-associated cues while the drug is withheld, to extinguish the association; the author proposes that it would be more effective if it also included internal cues (drug-onset and self-administration cues). No trial of this proposal is cited.
The review contains no data on overdose in people and does not cite the author's 1984 interviews with overdose survivors.

reporting_issues.issue: Several statements about people are made without a human study being named: greater tolerance to opiates when self-administered (p. 298) and the claim that small doses frequently precipitate withdrawal and relapse, called well established with one self-citation (p. 299).
reporting_issues.consequence: These statements cannot be cited from this review as human findings.

reporting_issues.issue: The caffeine example is cited partly to a one-page item in Circulation (2003, vol. 108, e38) by the author's group.
reporting_issues.consequence: The human caffeine evidence cannot be judged from this review; check the primary report before citing it.
